chunks: My father narrated to us, may God be pleased with him, saying: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar narrated to us, saying: Ayyub ibn Nooh narrated to me, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Musa ibn Bakr al-Wasiti, who said: I asked Abul Hasan Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon them both): If a man says to his son or daughter, 'May my father and mother be your ransom' or 'May my parents be your ransom,' do you see anything wrong with that? He replied: If his parents are alive, I consider that to be ingratitude (uquq), but if they have died, there is no harm. He said: Then he said: Ja'far (peace be upon him) used to say: A man is prosperous if he lives to see his successor after him. And by God, God has shown me my successor after me.

key_terms.بِأَبِي أَنْتَ وَامِي: A phrase meaning 'May my father and mother be your ransom' (a term of endearment)
key_terms.خَلْفِي: My successor or successor after me

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on saying 'Abuka wa Ummuka' to children in Shia tradition?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq records this hadith in *Al-Khisal* to illustrate the transition from filial piety to parental pride, noting that the phrase becomes an act of ingratitude (*uquq*) if parents are alive, as it implies a desire to replace them, but is permissible after death. The Imam’s affirmation that he was shown his successor refers specifically to Imam Musa al-Kadhim (peace be upon him), highlighting the continuity of the Imamate and the spiritual prosperity of witnessing the next generation's leadership. This narrative underscores the Shia emphasis on the sanctity of the Imams' lineage and the virtue of living to see the establishment of one's progeny in authority.
